title: Duryodhana's Lavish Pavilions That Krishna Ignores
story:
News of Krishna's journey reached the Kuru palace before Krishna did. Dhritarashtra, the blind king, learned from his spies that the slayer of Madhu had set out, and his hair stood on end. He called Bhishma, Drona, Sanjaya, and the wise Vidura, and spoke to Duryodhana and his counsellors.

"Strange and wonderful is the news we hear," he said. "Men, women, and children are talking of it, in the houses where men congregate and in open spots. All say that Dasarha of great prowess will come here for the sake of the Pandavas. The slayer of Madhu deserves honour and worship at our hands. He is the Lord of all creatures; on him rests the course of everything in the universe. Intelligence, prowess, wisdom, and energy — all reside in Madhava. Worthy of honour at the hands of all righteous persons, he is the foremost of all men, eternal Virtue itself. If worshipped, he is sure to bestow happiness; if not worshipped, he is sure to inflict misery. If Dasarha is gratified with our offerings, all our wishes may be obtained through his grace in the midst of the kings. Make every arrangement for his reception without loss of time. Let pavilions be set up on the road, furnished with every object of enjoyment. Make such arrangements that he may be gratified with you. What does Bhishma think in this matter?"

Bhishma and the others applauded the king's words. "Excellent," they said.

And Duryodhana, understanding their wishes, ordered delightful sites to be chosen for the erection of pavilions. Many pavilions were thereupon constructed, abounding with gems of every kind, at proper intervals and at delightful spots along the route. The king sent handsome seats of excellent quality, beautiful girls, scents and ornaments, fine robes, excellent viands, drinks of diverse qualities, and fragrant garlands of many kinds. He took especial care to erect, for Krishna's reception, one highly beautiful pavilion at Vrikasthala, full of precious gems. When all was done — arrangements godlike, far above the capacity of human beings — Duryodhana informed Dhritarashtra that everything was ready.

The road from Vrikasthala to the capital had been turned into a pageant. Pavilions rose at proper intervals, each one a small palace of gems, and the air along the way carried the weight of garlands, scents, and vessels of drink laid out for a king's welcome. Travellers and citizens alike slowed to look at what Duryodhana had built, and the talk was all of the wealth being spent to receive one man.

Then Kesava arrived at the capital of the Kurus.

And he passed all of it by: the gem-studded pavilions, the seats, the garlands, the viands, the whole costly display raised in his honour — without casting a single glance at it. Not one of the gems of diverse kinds drew his eyes. The contrast was there for the whole city to see. Duryodhana had built as though the visitor could be dazzled into alliance, as though magnificence itself were the language in which the Kurus and the Pandavas could still be reconciled. Krishna, who needed nothing, made the whole architecture of the welcome irrelevant as his chariot rolled past the last pavilion and on toward the city — and a court that had measured him in gold was left, at his silent passing, to wonder what measure would have been right.
reflection: The reception is measured entirely in riches, and Krishna's answer is perfect indifference: the gifts say everything about the giver and nothing about the guest. A man who needs nothing cannot be won by display — only by the truthfulness of the one who receives him.
next_story_tease: When Dhritarashtra began planning gifts meant to bind Krishna, Vidura would name the deception openly.
hero_scene: Krishna's chariot passes gem-studded pavilions hung with garlands along the road to Hastinapura, his eyes fixed straight ahead, while the assembled display of seats, vessels, and ornaments stands ignored and unused.
